title: How to Inoculate Yourself Against Edtech Psychosis
author: Meyer, Dan
summary: Dan Meyer diagnoses a recurring pattern he calls 'edtech psychosis' — school districts and companies whipsawing between promoting and banning AI tools within the space of a year or two — and argues the cure is direct, regular time in real classrooms rather than more conference talks or LinkedIn takes. He traces the condition to a specific incentive structure: tech companies' free cash flow meeting schools' threadbare budgets, combined with people whose pedagogical convictions are too weak to resist whatever novel technology walks by. As his own inoculation, he announces he has talked his way into a weekly fifth-grade classroom placement for the year. The piece closes with several sharp asides, including a rebuttal of Microsoft president Brad Smith's framing of corporate edtech philanthropy as filling a gap the public sector failed to fill, and a school-board member's observation that laptop-and-headphone independent work has quietly eliminated in-classroom peer conversation.
points: Coins 'edtech psychosis' for the whiplash pattern of districts promoting then banning the same AI tools within a year or two.
Argues the condition is diagnosable: people impressed more by novel business models than by good teaching or curriculum design.
Prescribes a concrete, personal inoculation — regular weekly time actually teaching or observing in a classroom — over conference talks or online commentary.
Rebuts the framing that corporate edtech philanthropy 'fills a gap' left by public education, calling it a subsidy for corporate employee-development costs instead.
Notes that laptop-and-headphone independent work can eliminate peer-to-peer classroom conversation entirely, which a school board member found viscerally 'odd' once she actually watched it happen.
quotes: Edtech psychosis flourishes wherever a giant tech company's free cash flow meets education's threadbare operating budgets. Edtech psychosis flourishes in people who are more impressed by a novel business model or a speculative technology than by good teaching or a well-designed curriculum.

You'll imagine students as little empty hard drives or young disobedient employees. You'll imagine teachers as frantic CPUs, desperately trying to write different bits of information onto every student.

Immunocompetent people understand the "grammar of schooling"—the goals, constraints, routines, and aspirations that power the people who work in schools. The immunocompromised do none of those things.
Time in classrooms keeps my imagination pointed at the actual rather than imagined problems of kids and teachers. It keeps me inoculated against edtech psychosis.

Philanthropy in the private sector is doing this work because the public sector has failed to do what it's supposed to do," Mr. Smith said. He allowed that the situation wasn't ideal. "It's filled the gap out of necessity," he said.
Of course public education doesn't operate the way you want it to, Brad. Private industry has always wanted the public to subsidize its employee development costs.
[Latta] said she has sometimes visited schools and seen entire classes of students not speaking to each other, but working independently on laptops with headphones on, which struck her as odd.
